edges.target: Loss of Glypican-3 Competition for Hedgehog Ligand

edges.source: Loss of Glypican-3 Competition for Hedgehog Ligand

edges.description: The null mouse reproduces the developmental overgrowth together with several other features of the human syndrome, including cystic and dysplastic kidneys and abnormal lung development.
edges.limitations: Perinatal death in a proportion of mutants limits the study of postnatal and later childhood phenotypes, and the tumor predisposition that defines the human syndrome is not part of the reported phenotype.

edges.description: The model does not reproduce what the IGF2 sequestration hypothesis predicts. If glypican-3 restrained IGF-II by binding it, removing glypican-3 should raise ligand levels; in the null mouse they are unchanged.
edges.limitations: A negative ligand level result does not exclude a local or compartment specific effect on IGF-II availability that a whole animal measurement would miss, so this refutes simple sequestration rather than every possible IGF2 mechanism.

evidence.snippet: distinctive craniofacial features (including macrocephaly, coarse facial features, macrostomia, macroglossia, and palate abnormalities)

nodes.description: Structural cardiac malformation. Cardiac involvement is singled out in the clinical utility gene card as needing longitudinal follow up beyond the detection of a defect at diagnosis, because conduction and rhythm problems develop later and contribute to premature death.

evidence.snippet: Other variable findings include supernumerary nipples, diastasis recti / umbilical hernia, congenital heart defects, diaphragmatic hernia, genitourinary defects, and gastrointestinal issues.
In addition to the detection of heart defects at the time of the diagnosis, a regular cardiac follow-up is necessary in order to detect and treat heart conduction and rhythm problems.

nodes.description: Increased proliferation in developing mesodermal tissues. In the kidney this was localized to the ureteric bud and collecting system in the null mouse, giving an early and persistent developmental abnormality rather than a purely postnatal growth excess.

evidence.reference_title: Glypican-3-deficient mice exhibit developmental overgrowth and some of the abnormalities typical of Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome.
evidence.snippet: In the particular case of the kidney, we demonstrate that there is an early and persistent developmental abnormality of the ureteric bud/collecting system due to increased proliferation of cells in this tissue element.

nodes.description: Hemizygous loss of function of GPC3 through point mutation, intragenic microdeletion, whole gene deletion, or translocation breakpoint disruption removes functional glypican-3 from the cell surface of embryonic mesodermal tissues, where it is selectively expressed.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in GPC3, a glypican gene, cause the Simpson-Golabi-Behmel overgrowth syndrome.
evidence.snippet: The breakpoints occur near the 5' and 3' ends of a gene, GPC3, that spans more than 500 kilobases in Xq26; in three families, different microdeletions encompassing exons cosegregate with SGBS.

evidence.reference_title: Mutational analysis of the GPC3/GPC4 glypican gene cluster on Xq26 in patients with Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome: identification of loss-of-function mutations in the GPC3 gene.
evidence.snippet: One frameshift, three nonsense, and one splice mutation predict a loss-of-function of the glypican-3 protein.

genetic_context.description: Loss of function alleles of GPC3 spanning point mutations, intragenic and whole gene deletions, and X;autosome translocation breakpoints that disrupt the locus.

nodes.description: The organism level consequence, expressed as macrosomia, macrocephaly, visceromegaly, and the characteristic coarse facies.

animal_models.description: The null mouse reproduces the developmental overgrowth together with several other features of the human syndrome, including cystic and dysplastic kidneys and abnormal lung development.
animal_models.name: Gpc3-null mouse

evidence.reference_title: Glypican-3-deficient mice exhibit developmental overgrowth and some of the abnormalities typical of Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome.
evidence.snippet: we report that GPC3-deficient mice exhibit several of the clinical features observed in SGBS patients, including developmental overgrowth, perinatal death, cystic and dyplastic kidneys, and abnormal lung development.

nodes.description: The loss of function mouse that established GPC3 as sufficient for the overgrowth phenotype and that produced the ligand level result which undercut the IGF2 sequestration model.

Released Hedgehog signaling raises the growth set point in embryonic tissues. Hedgehog positively regulates body size, so its de-repression is the proposed proximate driver of the overgrowth phenotype.

evidence.reference_title: Glypican-3 inhibits Hedgehog signaling during development by competing with patched for Hedgehog binding.
evidence.snippet: We conclude that GPC3 acts as a negative regulator of Hedgehog signaling during mammalian development and that the overgrowth observed in SGBS patients is, at least in part, the consequence of hyperactivation of the Hedgehog signaling pathway.
Screening for Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma with abdominal ultrasound and serum AFP level every three months from time of diagnosis until age three years

nodes.description: The originally proposed mechanism, in which glypican-3 forms a complex with IGF2 and restrains its growth promoting action. It is recorded here because much of the older literature assumes it, but the ligand level data from the null mouse do not support a simple sequestration model. It is deliberately left unconnected to the downstream chain, since the evidence does not license an edge.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in GPC3, a glypican gene, cause the Simpson-Golabi-Behmel overgrowth syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Initial western- and ligand-blotting experiments suggest that glypican 3 forms a complex with insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2), and might thereby modulate IGF2 action.

evidence.reference_title: Glypican-3-deficient mice exhibit developmental overgrowth and some of the abnormalities typical of Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Unlike the IGF2R-deficient mice, however, the levels of IGF-II in GPC3 knockouts are similar to those of the normal littermates.

nodes.description: Detection of structural heart defects at diagnosis, followed by ongoing cardiac review for conduction and rhythm disturbance. This is the only condition specific longitudinal surveillance besides tumor screening, and the clinical utility gene card links it to premature death.

evidence.snippet: In addition to the detection of heart defects at the time of the diagnosis, a regular cardiac follow-up is necessary in order to detect and treat heart conduction and rhythm problems.

nodes.description: Glypican-3 binds Hedgehog with high affinity and competes with Patched, the Hedgehog receptor, for that ligand, then routes the bound Hedgehog to endocytosis and degradation. Without glypican-3 this sink is gone and more ligand reaches Patched.
nodes.id: Loss of Glypican-3 Competition for Hedgehog Ligand

evidence.reference_title: Glypican-3 inhibits Hedgehog signaling during development by competing with patched for Hedgehog binding.
evidence.snippet: we report that GPC3 interacts with high affinity with Hedgehog but not with its receptor, Patched, and that GPC3 competes with Patched for Hedgehog binding. Furthermore, GPC3 induces Hedgehog endocytosis and degradation.
distinctive craniofacial features (including macrocephaly, coarse facial features, macrostomia, macroglossia, and palate abnormalities)
monitoring of serum glucose level in the neonatal period

nodes.description: The two urgent neonatal problems. Hypoglycemia requires prompt correction and glucose monitoring through the neonatal period; airway obstruction arises from micrognathia and glossoptosis and may require positioning or airway support.

evidence.snippet: Prompt treatment of neonatal hypoglycemia and airway obstruction resulting from micrognathia and glossoptosis.

nodes.description: Wilms tumor, the commonest embryonal tumor in this syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals are at increased risk for embryonal tumors including Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma, adrenal neuroblastoma, gonadoblastoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and medulloblastoma.

nodes.description: Pre- and postnatal macrosomia, the defining growth phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome type 1 (SGBS1) is characterized by pre- and postnatal macrosomia

nodes.description: Retained embryonal progenitor populations, notably nephrogenic rests in the kidney and hepatic progenitors in the liver, are the substrate on which the childhood embryonal tumors of this syndrome arise. This is why tumor surveillance is concentrated in the first years of life.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals are at increased risk for embryonal tumors including Wilms tumor, hepatoblastoma, adrenal neuroblastoma, gonadoblastoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, and medulloblastoma.

nodes.description: Enlargement of the abdominal viscera, part of the generalized overgrowth and asserted in this entry's own description of the overgrowth node.

evidence.snippet: Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome (SGBS) is an X-linked multiple congenital anomalies (MCA) and overgrowth syndrome characterized in males by foetal macrosomia, postnatal overgrowth, macrocephaly, organomegaly

nodes.description: Abdominal ultrasound with serum alpha fetoprotein every three months from diagnosis to age three years for Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma, then renal ultrasound every three months to age seven years. No protocol has been established for the rarer tumors in the spectrum, which are instead covered by six monthly review with a cancer predisposition specialist.

evidence.snippet: Screening for Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma with abdominal ultrasound and serum AFP level every three months from time of diagnosis until age three years; renal ultrasound every three months until age seven years
no specific tumor screening protocol has been established for neuroblastoma, gonadoblastoma, or medulloblastoma, but follow up with a cancer predisposition specialist every six months is recommended
